title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Strategies For Food Production — 2025
origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 strategies for enhancement in food production unit

questions.question: What is plant breeding? Describe its main steps.
questions.solution:
Plant breeding is the deliberate genetic improvement of crop plants to raise yield and quality, and to add resistance to disease, pests and stress.
Steps: (1) collection and evaluation of genetic variability — germplasm collection from wild relatives and landraces; (2) selection of parents with the desired characters; (3) hybridisation — crossing them to combine traits; (4) selection in the segregating generations, often by pedigree or bulk method, until the line is uniform; (5) testing for yield, quality and resistance in multi-location trials; (6) release and seed multiplication. Mutation breeding, polyploidy and, more recently, marker-assisted selection and genetic engineering speed up or widen the process.

questions.question: Explain the types of hybridisation used in plant breeding and give two achievements of the green revolution in India and Nepal.
questions.solution:
Hybridisation may be intraspecific (crossing two varieties of the same species), interspecific (two species of a genus) or intergeneric (two genera, used to transfer disease resistance from wild relatives). It may be a simple cross, a back-cross to recover the recurrent parent, or a three-way and double cross in self-pollinated crops.
Achievements: semi-dwarf, fertiliser-responsive Mexican wheat (Sonora-64, Lerma Rojo) and IR8 rice raised yields several-fold and made the green revolution possible; in Nepal improved rice (Radha-4, Sabitri) and wheat varieties spread widely, and hybrid maize and disease-resistant varieties raised production — though at the cost of heavier input use.

questions.question: What is single cell protein? Name two organisms used and give its advantages.
questions.solution:
Single cell protein (SCP) is protein extracted from the cells of microorganisms — algae, yeasts, fungi or bacteria — grown in bulk culture and used as a protein-rich food or feed supplement.
Organisms: the alga Spirulina and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae; also Methylophilus methylotrophus (bacterium) and the fungus Fusarium.
Advantages: fast growth gives high yield on cheap substrates including waste (molasses, whey, methanol, straw hydrolysate); it is rich in protein and B vitamins and can be produced in a small area independent of weather; it recycles waste and reduces pollution. Limits are the cost of processing, possible nucleic acid excess and consumer acceptance.

questions.question: Describe animal husbandry with reference to cattle breeds and poultry management.
questions.solution:
Animal husbandry is the scientific management of farm animals — feeding, breeding, housing, health care and record keeping — to obtain milk, meat, eggs, wool and draught power.
Cattle: indigenous breeds such as Sahiwal and Red Sindhi (disease-resistant, good for hot climates) and exotic Jersey and Holstein-Friesian (high milk yield) are crossed for combined merit; breeding is by artificial insemination, with attention to balanced feed, clean water, housing and vaccination against foot-and-mouth and haemorrhagic septicaemia.
Poultry: layers such as Leghorn and broilers such as Plymouth Rock are raised with controlled temperature, balanced feed, clean litter, vaccination against Ranikhet and culling of diseased birds.

questions.question: What are biofertilisers? Name three types and state their advantages.
questions.solution:
Biofertilisers are preparations of living microorganisms that enrich the soil with nutrients, mainly nitrogen or phosphorus, when applied to seed or soil.
Types: nitrogen-fixing bacteria — Rhizobium (symbiotic in legume root nodules) and Azotobacter and Azospirillum (free-living); cyanobacteria such as Anabaena and Azolla (used in paddy fields); phosphate-solubilising bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi, which make insoluble phosphorus available.
Advantages: they are cheap, renewable and non-polluting, reduce the need for chemical nitrogen, improve soil structure and water holding, and are suited to small farmers; they have no harmful residues and often suppress soil-borne pathogens.

questions.question: What is sustainable agriculture? Give four practices that make agriculture sustainable.
questions.solution:
Sustainable agriculture is farming that meets present food needs without damaging the soil, water, biodiversity or climate on which future production depends — it balances productivity with ecological and social costs.
Practices: crop rotation and mixed cropping with legumes to restore nitrogen; use of organic manure, compost and biofertilisers instead of only chemical fertiliser; integrated pest management with biological control and resistant varieties; conservation of soil and water by terracing, contour bunding and mulching; and agroforestry, drip irrigation and use of local seed to reduce inputs and risk.
